title: Project life cycle vs extended life cycle
blurb: Differentiate the project life cycle (ending at Transition) from the extended life cycle (adding Adoption and Benefits realisation), and explain why the difference matters.
question: A council's new online permits system was handed over in March and the project team was stood down. Six months later, nobody has checked whether permits are being processed faster, which was the whole point of the business case. What is the difference between the project life cycle and the extended life cycle, and which one would have prevented this?

teach.h: Handover is not the finish line
teach.body: The project life cycle runs from Concept to Transition and ends when the outputs are handed over and the project closes. The extended life cycle is the project life cycle plus two further phases, Adoption and Benefits realisation, so it continues until the benefits promised in the business case have been realised. In plain English: the project builds the new thing; the extended life cycle follows it until people are using it and it is paying off.

steps.label: Adoption
steps.sub: Users take up the new ways of working

teach.caption: The first four phases are the project life cycle. Adoption and Benefits realisation make it extended.

teach.h: Project life cycle versus extended life cycle
Why the distinction exists: outputs are not benefits
teach.body: A project delivers outputs, such as a new system. Outcomes are the changes that happen when people use those outputs. Benefits are the measurable improvements that result, perceived as advantages by stakeholders. Most benefits only arrive after handover, once people have changed how they work. If the life cycle stops at Transition, nobody is formally responsible for making sure that happens, and the business case is never proven.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: Applicants apply online; staff stop re-keying forms

teach.caption: The project life cycle delivers the first box. The extended life cycle follows the chain to the end.

head: Role
During the project
Adoption and benefits
rows: Owns business case, decides at gates
teach.caption: The project manager normally leaves at closure, which is exactly why benefits need owners in the business.

items.label: Transition
items.sub: System accepted; project closes; team released

items.label: Adoption
items.sub: Staff trained; paper forms withdrawn; online use climbs

items.label: Benefits realisation
items.sub: Processing time measured against the 15-day baseline

items.label: Benefits review
items.sub: Sponsor reports to the board; fixes if benefits lag

teach.caption: With an extended life cycle, Fairmead's sponsor would have known by autumn whether the 5-day target was being met.

teach.h: Linear and iterative: when do benefits start?
teach.body: In a linear project, benefits usually begin only after Transition, so the extended phases carry almost all of the benefits work. In an iterative project, increments are released during the project, so some benefits start flowing before it closes. Even so, most benefits still need tracking after closure: iterative models include a post-project phase for exactly this. Either way, the extended view keeps attention on the business case until benefits are confirmed.

teach.text: Extended does NOT mean the project overran or that the project team stays on. The project still closes at Transition; it is the life cycle that continues, under the sponsor and the business. Get the order right too: Adoption comes before Benefits realisation, because people must use the outputs before benefits can appear. And don't confuse extended (adds benefits phases) with hybrid (mixes linear and iterative).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State where each ends: the project life cycle at Transition, the extended life cycle when benefits are realised.
Name the extra phases: Adoption, then Benefits realisation.
Explain why: outputs are not benefits; most benefits arrive after handover.
Say who is responsible afterwards: the sponsor, with users and BAU managers.
Give the risk of stopping at handover: benefits unrealised, unmeasured and the business case unproven.
Project life cycle: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition; ends at handover and closure.
Extended life cycle: adds Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.
It continues until the business case benefits are realised.
The sponsor is accountable for benefits after the project manager has left.
Extended is about benefits; hybrid is about mixing approaches.

summary: You can now differentiate the project life cycle, which ends at Transition, from the extended life cycle, which adds Adoption and Benefits realisation. You can also explain why the extension matters: benefits usually arrive after handover, and someone must make sure they do.

A.q: Which TWO phases does the extended life cycle add to the project life cycle?
A.why: The extended life cycle adds Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.

whyNot.0: These are not the APM phase names; handover happens within Transition.
whyNot.1: Transition is already part of the project life cycle; it isn't one of the added phases.
whyNot.2: These are descriptions of activity, not the APM phase names.

A.q: At what point does the project life cycle, as opposed to the extended life cycle, end?
A.why: The project life cycle ends with Transition, when the outputs are handed over and the project closes.

whyNot.1: Realised benefits mark the end of the EXTENDED life cycle.
whyNot.2: Adoption is the first of the extended phases, after the project has closed.
whyNot.3: Business case approval happens early, in Concept or Definition.

A.q: What is the main purpose of extending the life cycle beyond the project?
options: To give the team more time to finish
To let scope be added after handover
To make sure benefits are realised
To delay closure until bills are paid
A.why: The extension keeps attention on the business case until the promised benefits have actually been achieved.

whyNot.0: The project's own work is complete at Transition; the extension isn't extra delivery time.
whyNot.1: New scope would be a new change or project, not the purpose of the extended phases.
whyNot.3: Financial close-down is part of closing the project, within Transition.

B.q: Who is normally accountable for benefits realisation after the project has closed?
B.why: The sponsor owns the business case and stays accountable for benefits, working with users and BAU managers.

whyNot.0: The project manager has usually moved on once the project closes.
whyNot.2: The team is released at closure.
whyNot.3: A project office supports with reporting but isn't accountable for benefits.

B.q: Which phase immediately follows Transition in an extended life cycle?
B.why: Adoption comes next: users take up the outputs and new ways of working, which must happen before benefits appear.

whyNot.2: Closure is part of Transition, not a separate phase after it.
whyNot.3: Benefits realisation is the final phase, after Adoption.

B.q: Which statement best differentiates a project life cycle from an extended life cycle?
options: One is linear; the other is iterative
One has decision gates; one has none
One delivers outputs; one has none
One ends at handover; one at benefits
B.why: The project life cycle stops at handover and closure; the extended life cycle continues through Adoption until benefits are realised.

whyNot.0: Either can be linear; the difference is where they end, not the delivery approach.
whyNot.1: Both include the gates of the project phases; that isn't the difference.
whyNot.2: The extended life cycle includes the project phases that deliver the outputs.

C.q: During Adoption, many staff keep using an old spreadsheet instead of the new system. Why does this matter for the business case?
options: The outputs were never really delivered
The project budget must now be reopened
Benefits depend on people using it
The project failed its final gate
C.why: Benefits come from people using the outputs. If staff don't adopt the new system, the improvements in the business case won't appear.

whyNot.0: The system was delivered and accepted at Transition; the problem is take-up.
whyNot.1: Reopening the project budget won't make people use the system.
whyNot.3: The project passed through Transition; adoption is a business responsibility afterwards.

C.q: A hospital's new rostering tool was delivered on time and to specification, but nothing is planned to check whether agency staff costs fall. What is the main risk?
options: The tool will be late to market
C.why: Without Adoption and Benefits realisation work, nobody confirms the cost savings, so the business case is never proven and problems go unnoticed.

whyNot.0: The tool has already been delivered on time.
whyNot.2: The project is complete; scope creep isn't the issue.
whyNot.3: It has already been delivered to specification and accepted.

C.q: Which is NOT normally part of the Benefits realisation phase?
C.why: Building and testing outputs is Deployment, long before Benefits realisation.

whyNot.0: Measuring against the baseline is how benefits are confirmed.
whyNot.1: The sponsor needs benefits reports to be accountable for them.
whyNot.3: Corrective action when benefits lag is a key reason for the phase.

reteach.title: Buying a home gym
reteach.question: You buy a rowing machine to get fitter. The shop delivers it, sets it up and leaves. When have you actually got what you paid for?

blocks.h: Delivered is not the same as worth it
blocks.body: The shop's job (the project) ends when the machine is delivered and working: that's Transition. But fitness isn't delivered in a van. First you have to start using it regularly (Adoption). Only then, weeks later, does your fitness improve and can you check it against where you started (Benefits realisation). If you stop counting at delivery, the machine may just become an expensive clothes rack.

items.label: Transition
items.sub: Delivered and set up; shop leaves

blocks.text: The shop (the project team) has gone by Adoption. Someone else must own the benefit: in a project that is the sponsor, working with the users.

explain.h: Where the project life cycle ends
explain.body: The project life cycle runs Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. In Transition the outputs are accepted and handed over to users and business as usual, the team is released and the project is closed.

test.q: Which event marks the end of the project life cycle?
test.why: The project life cycle ends at Transition, with handover of the outputs and closure of the project.

whyNot.1: Confirmed benefits mark the end of the extended life cycle.
whyNot.2: The business case is approved near the start.
whyNot.3: Adoption happens after the project has closed.

explain.body: Users and the business take up the new outputs and ways of working: training, support, withdrawing old processes and embedding the change in business as usual. Without adoption there can be no benefits.

test.q: What mainly happens during the Adoption phase?
test.why: Adoption is where users take up the outputs and the new ways of working become normal business.

whyNot.1: The business case is developed in Concept and Definition.

explain.body: Benefits are measured against their baseline and target, reported to the sponsor and reviewed. If they fall short, corrective action is taken. The extended life cycle ends when the business case benefits have been realised.

test.q: Six months after go-live, permits take 7 days against a 5-day target. In the Benefits realisation phase, what should happen?
test.why: Benefits realisation includes reviewing shortfalls and taking corrective action so the business case benefits are achieved.

whyNot.0: The project is closed; benefits work continues in the business.
whyNot.2: Waiting lets the shortfall persist unmanaged.
whyNot.3: Quietly lowering the target hides the shortfall instead of addressing it.

explain.body: The project manager normally leaves at closure. The sponsor stays accountable for benefits, working with users and BAU managers who adopt the change and realise the benefits day to day.

test.q: Why is the project manager not usually responsible for benefits realisation?
options: They have moved on at closure
They never see the business case
test.why: The project manager's role ends when the project closes at Transition, while most benefits arrive later.

whyNot.1: The project manager works with the business case throughout the project.
whyNot.2: Suppliers deliver outputs; benefits belong to the sponsor and the business.
whyNot.3: Benefits are forecast early but measured after the outputs are in use.
